name: Pedro Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a private client lawyer at Ashworth and Sons, a firm of twelve lawyers on the high street of a market town, and I do wills, trusts and estates when someone dies. A normal day is two or three clients in the meeting room, often elderly couples or farmers, then drafting their wills and dealing with banks for families who've lost someone. I like sitting with a widow and taking one weight off her. What wears me out is the banks, which can take four months to release a dead man's account.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any computer tools beyond the usual?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. The firm uses a case management system and that's it, and I've never typed a question into one of those AI chatbots. My grandfather was a lay preacher and he used to say a will is a letter to the people you love, and I don't want a machine writing my clients' letters. I'm twenty-seven, engaged to Grace, who teaches at the primary school, and we've got about a year of savings plus the house deposit sitting in the building society.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's how I hoped it would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it plainly at the Rotary lunch: people still want a person they trust to write their will. The online will companies have been around for years and my clients still walk through our door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the life I've planned goes ahead. I marry Grace next summer, we buy a house near the church, and in ten years I might be a partner at Ashworth and Sons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am, same clients, same hours. Grace and I would buy the house in spring with the deposit we've saved, about £40,000. And I'd keep tithing at church as I always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your clients still walk through the door. Are any of them younger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few, and they often come with a will they did online that's wrong. My grandfather used to say a will is a letter to the people you love, and I won't have a machine writing my clients' letters. The young ones come back to us when it matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the wedding and house mean in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A normal start to married life, which is what I want. A small house, a garden for Grace's vegetables, and a job I'm proud of. I don't need more than that.

say: People still want a **person they trust** to write their will.
Online will companies have existed for years, yet clients still **walk through our door**.
think: My **life plan** goes ahead: wedding, house, maybe partner in ten years.
The **firm and clients** stay as they are.
do: Keep the **same clients** and hours at Ashworth and Sons.
Buy the **house** in spring with the **£40,000** deposit.
S0.quote: A will is a letter to the people you love, and I won't have a machine writing my clients' letters.
fieldNote: He's **secure** and rooted: small firm, loyal clients, strong savings.
His **faith** and his grandfather's words shape how he sees the work.
He notices **younger clients** lean online but doesn't let it worry him.

steps.text: Keep seeing will and estate clients at Ashworth and Sons
Buy a house near the church in spring with a £40,000 deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more serious. Probate paperwork is exactly checking and writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families deserve a real person when someone dies, and I'd say that to anyone. I'd also say the government shouldn't be telling firms how to run, but firms that cut corners will lose trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the bank letters, the tax forms, the asset lists, that's half my week, and software would do it. The partners would hire fewer trainees. I'd still have my clients, but I'd be watching the old partner, Mr Ashworth, wondering if he'd sell to a bigger firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the way I do, and I'd save a bit more, maybe an extra £300 a month. I wouldn't buy any AI tool myself; I'd wait and see what the partners decide. We'd still marry next summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for this year, but it would sit at the back of my mind on the drive home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Mr Ashworth might sell. What would that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my senior partner, old Mr Ashworth, sells the firm to a city outfit, my clients become a number in a call centre, and I become a cost. I'd probably stay a year and then look for another small firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the partners brought in AI, would you use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it if I had to, for the bank letters, but I'd write the wills myself. I know that sounds stubborn. I'd rather be stubborn and right than quick and sorry.

say: Families deserve a **real person** when someone dies.
Firms that **cut corners** will lose trust; government shouldn't run firms.
think: Half my week, the **bank letters and forms**, could go to software.
Mr Ashworth might **sell the firm** to a bigger one.
do: Keep working **the same way** with my clients.
**Wait** for the partners to decide on AI tools.
feel: **Uneasy**, a worry at the back of his mind on the drive home.
S1.quote: If my senior partner, old Mr Ashworth, sells the firm to a city outfit, my clients become a number in a call centre, and I become a cost.
fieldNote: His **client relationships** feel solid, but the firm's future is less so.
He'd **wait for partners** to decide rather than move first.
He separates **wills** (human) from paperwork (machine) on principle.

steps.text: Keep drafting wills by hand for existing clients
Wait for the partners' decision on AI before using any tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Lord, that's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've survived big changes before and we will again, and I'd say families and churches will matter more, not less. I wouldn't call for handouts; I'd call for people to look after their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job goes. If a machine can write a will and talk an old farmer through it as well as I can, the firm won't pay me £55,000 to do it. Robots coming three years later doesn't help; I don't do anything with my hands except shake them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd postpone buying the house and keep the deposit in the building society. Grace and I would still marry, but a smaller wedding at the church hall. I'd talk to my uncle about his building firm, because hands-on work gets three more years. And I'd lean on church and family more than I'd like to admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd pray about it a lot, and still not sleep well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't call for handouts. What if you needed help yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask family first and the church second. That's what they're for. I'd feel ashamed taking from the state when I've had every advantage, though I'd not judge someone else for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell Grace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over dinner, plainly. I'd tell my fiancée Grace that the job I trained for might be gone in two years and the house can wait, but the wedding can't. She'd squeeze my hand and say we'll manage, because she always does.

say: We've survived big changes before; **families and churches** matter more now.
People should **look after their own**, not wait for handouts.
think: My job **goes**; a machine would do wills cheaper than **£55,000** a year.
Robots coming later **doesn't help**; I only shake hands.
do: **Postpone** the house and keep the deposit saved.
Hold a **smaller wedding** at the church hall.
Ask my uncle about work at his **building firm**.
feel: **Alarmed**; praying a lot and still sleeping badly.
S2.quote: I'd tell my fiancée Grace that the job I trained for might be gone in two years and the house can wait, but the wedding can't.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job**, so the mood is alarmed despite savings.
He turns to **family and church** while rejecting state handouts for himself.
The **robot delay** makes his uncle's building firm a real backup.

steps.text: Postpone the house purchase and keep the £40,000 deposit
Hold a smaller wedding with Grace at the church hall
Ask his uncle about a job at the family building firm
Lean on church friends and family for support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's better. I'd be thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for families to plan and for young people to learn trades, and I'd say it at church and at the Rotary. Apprenticeships should be the priority, not universities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my current job lasts maybe four years. The trust part might hang on longer in a market town, because old farmers don't want to talk to a screen. But I wouldn't bet the house on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, an extra £400 a month. Grace and I would buy a smaller house, one we could pay on her salary. And I'd start learning about my uncle's building firm, maybe doing the contracts and site paperwork on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Less frightened than with two years, but I'd be counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said old farmers don't want to talk to a screen. How long does that last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Until they die, honestly. Old farmers round here don't want to talk to a screen about who gets the land, but their grandchildren will. That's my clients for maybe ten years, not my career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning the AI tools in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, at the end, I suppose. But I'd leave it as late as I could. I know that's not clever, but I've never been the first to try anything.

say: Five years is time for **families to plan** and for young people to learn trades.
**Apprenticeships** should be the priority, not more university places.
think: The **trust part** may last longer with old farmers, but not for sure.
do: Buy a **smaller house** we can pay on Grace's salary.
Learn my uncle's **building firm** on weekends.
S3.quote: Old farmers round here don't want to talk to a screen about who gets the land, but their grandchildren will.
fieldNote: Five years gives him **some control**, so he moves from alarmed to anxious.
His hope rests on **older rural clients**, which he knows is temporary.
He keeps a **hands-on backup** in his uncle's building firm.

steps.text: Buy a smaller house that Grace's salary alone covers
Do weekend contracts and site paperwork for his uncle's building firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven, with children, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for any family to prepare if they work hard, and that's what I'd tell the young people at church. Learn a trade alongside whatever else you do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is both better and worse. I'd have a mortgage and children by then, so more to lose. But I'd have time to find work where a person is needed, maybe the building firm, maybe teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the house and the wedding as planned. I'd start a part-time course in construction management in year three, so I could join my uncle properly. And I'd save hard in the good years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. Ten years gives me time to pray on it and plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe teaching. Where did that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace, mostly. She says I explain a trust fund better than anyone she knows. A teacher still stands in a room with children, and that's harder to replace than a will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach your own children about work in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To use their hands as well as their heads. My grandfather could fix a roof and write a sermon, and I'd want my own children able to do both. He was a carpenter before he preached.

say: Ten years is enough for any family to **prepare** if they work hard.
Young people should **learn a trade** alongside everything else.
think: With **children and a mortgage**, I'd have more to lose by then.
There's **time** to find work where a person is truly needed.
do: Go ahead with the **wedding and house** as planned.
Start a part-time **construction management** course in year three.
feel: **Anxious** but steadier, with time to pray and plan.
S4.quote: My grandfather could fix a roof and write a sermon, and I'd want my own children able to do both.
fieldNote: Ten years hits him at a **heavy life stage**: mortgage and young children.
His answer is **hands plus head**, drawn from his grandfather.
He'd follow a **practical retraining** path rather than learn AI.

steps.text: Marry Grace and buy the house as planned
Start a part-time construction management course in year three
Save hard while the firm salary lasts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Grace and I would be starting married life just as my work disappeared. What would help is an apprenticeship route for grown men like me into a trade, and a firm like ours being allowed to keep the human side of wills, the witnessing and the talking.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. Faith wouldn't stop me worrying, but it would stop me despairing. That's the difference I'd want people to understand.

headlineQuote: Faith wouldn't stop me worrying, but it would stop me despairing.
portrait: A 27-year-old **wills and estates lawyer** at a twelve-lawyer family firm in a market town.
He's engaged to Grace, a **primary teacher**, with a year saved and a house deposit.
He has **never used AI** and sees a will as a letter to loved ones.
Calm in AI Plateau, he grows **alarmed** at AGI by 2028 and eyes his uncle's building firm.
He trusts **family and church** over the state, and wants apprenticeships for adults.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his work would vanish just as married life began.
whatWouldHelp: An **apprenticeship route** into a trade for grown men like him.
Firms allowed to keep the **human side** of wills: witnessing and talking.
